The organization, the systems, the data and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the IT technician at Delmar Tax Advisors, a fictional accounting firm of 30 people who travel to clients in tax season.
handover: Laptops have Windows sign-in passwords but no disk encryption.
The firm's client portal still answers on plain HTTP.
howItWorks: The desk shows the ticket queue against the priority matrix and each service's status.
Move on a day at a time. A decision comes to you at each service review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Day 2: the taxi company's finder copies the tax files; a client's identity is used for a fraudulent return.
Day 3: a client's return is intercepted on a hotel network and altered before it reaches the portal.
Day 4: an unlocked phone left at a cafe gives a stranger access to a client's email thread with bank details.

restPrompt.title: A lost laptop without encryption
restPrompt.context: A sign-in password does not protect the disk.

choices.label: Turn on full-disk encryption on every laptop, escrow the recovery keys centrally, and report the lost laptop as a possible breach

effects.log: All laptops are encrypting; the loss is reported.

choices.feedback: Encryption at rest protects data on a lost device; a sign-in password alone does not, because the disk can be read elsewhere.

choices.label: Require longer sign-in passwords
choices.feedback: The disk can still be removed and read.

choices.label: Treat the lost laptop as hardware loss and order a new one
choices.feedback: Three clients' files are readable by whoever has the laptop.

transitPrompt.title: Client files over hotel Wi-Fi
transitPrompt.context: Staff upload files to the portal over plain HTTP from hotels.

choices.label: Serve the portal only over HTTPS with a valid certificate, redirect HTTP, and require the company VPN on untrusted networks

effects.log: Portal traffic is encrypted; the VPN is required away from the office.

choices.feedback: HTTPS encrypts web traffic in transit, and a VPN protects everything else on untrusted networks.

choices.label: Offer the VPN but leave the portal on HTTP
choices.feedback: Anyone who skips the VPN still sends files in plain text.

choices.label: Email staff to avoid hotel Wi-Fi
choices.feedback: Staff still have to work; files still cross in plain text.

mobilePrompt.title: Phones with client email
mobilePrompt.context: Nine phones have no screen lock.

choices.label: Require device encryption and a screen lock, and enroll phones that hold client email in mobile device management with remote wipe
choices.feedback: Mobile devices hold the same data as laptops; encryption, a lock and remote wipe protect it when a phone is lost.

choices.label: Require a screen lock only
choices.feedback: Better, but a lost phone cannot be wiped.

choices.label: Allow any phone with no requirements
choices.feedback: A lost unlocked phone opens client email to anyone.

reflection.question: Write the support record for the managing partner.

parts.label: At rest
parts.criteria: Full-disk encryption on all laptops; the loss reported.
parts.modelAnswer: Every laptop now encrypts its disk with recovery keys held centrally; the lost laptop was reported as a possible breach.

parts.label: In transit and mobile
parts.criteria: HTTPS portal, VPN on untrusted networks, managed phones.
parts.modelAnswer: The portal is HTTPS-only, the VPN is required away from the office, and phones are encrypted, locked and can be wiped.

scoring.modelReasoning: Encryption at rest (full-disk encryption) protects data on lost devices; encryption in transit (HTTPS, VPNs) protects data crossing untrusted networks; mobile devices need encryption, a lock and remote wipe. Passwords and advice alone do not protect the data.
